own_scenes.desc: La experiencia de monster funk más fuerte y auténtica de la década: en clubes de Washington como el Black Hole o el Coliseum, Trouble Funk, E.U., Rare Essence, Redds and the Boys y su mentor Chuck Brown & the Soul Searchers tocaban dos o tres «canciones» de una hora sobre un ritmo implacable: bajo lento y espeso, timbales y congas a contratiempo, vientos jazzísticos, cantos del público y trozos de éxitos, más cerca del reggae, el calipso y la salsa que de los singles. Para Nelson George, «música local con corazón internacional», nacida de la ironía de la miseria negra al lado del Capitolio. Chuck Brown encendió la escena con «Bustin’ Loose» (1978); Trouble Funk («Big Tony» Fisher y tres baterías) grabó «Pump Me Up» y «Drop the Bomb» para Sugarhill y «Trouble Funk Express», pero la película Good to Go fracasó e Island los maquilló como a Cameo. El go-go entró en Kurtis Blow, Doug E. Fresh o Salt-N-Pepa, y «Da Butt» de E.U. (School Daze de Spike Lee, de Marcus Miller) llegó al número 1 R&B en 1988.

influences.name: África responde: Manu Dibango y Fela Kuti

refs.q: The Go Go beat is hard-core funk
refs.para: The Go Go beat is hard-core funk—a thick and slow bass groove, overlayed with a relentless counterpunching timbale or conga beat, jazzy horn breaks, chants of audience participation, and catchy lyrics or riffs from well-known dance hits, all delivered with a raw edge that rejected the digitized notions of eighties R&B heard on the radio. While the Go Go beat is an urban funk explosion, the approach to the music had more to do with the endless rhythms of Afro-Caribbean dance styles such as reggae, calypso, and salsa—all of which thrive on rhythmic energy, rather than hit records.
refs.chapter: Cap. 20: Hip Hop and Black Noise: Raising Hell

refs.q: The beat is so simple most drummers don’t like to play it.
refs.para: The Godfather of the Go Go beat is Chuck Brown, bandleader of the Soul Searchers since 1968. A tireless performer, Brown made his mark playing club dates year after year, developing his particular brand of R&B, one with a simple, steady, nonstop funky groove on the bottom, with lots of room to operate and improvise on top. “I’d been trying to get drummers to play that particular groove for the longest time,” Brown told journalist Adam White. “The beat is so simple most drummers don’t like to play it.”
refs.chapter: Cap. 20: Hip Hop and Black Noise: Raising Hell

refs.q: A Trouble Funk performance was a required initiation for those who wanted to be ultimate funkateers.
refs.para: Independently producing themselves on TF Records, and later with the help (and hype) of Maxx Kidd and D.E.T.T. Records, Trouble Funk blasted ahead of the pack onto the D.C. Go Go scene. Featuring the loud and aggressive lead vocals of 250-plus-pound bass player and singer “Big Tony” Fisher, guitarist Robert “Dyke” Reed, and keyboardist James Avery, and always supporting at least three drummers, led by Timothy “T-Bone” David, Alonzo Robinson, and Mack Carey, Trouble Funk was a nonstop funk machine. The Trouble Funk groove was ferocious—and it never let up. Nine men strong, kicking a drum splattering, stupefying fat funk chunk from all directions, a Trouble Funk jam session burned the roof off the house. A Trouble Funk performance was a required initiation for those who wanted to be ultimate funkateers.
refs.chapter: Cap. 20: Hip Hop and Black Noise: Raising Hell

own_scenes.place: Estados Unidos (Peppermint Lounge, Whisky a Go Go)
own_scenes.desc: El Twist (1960-1962) fue el gran liberador del baile social: sin pareja, libre, con poco juego de pies; tras él llegó un aluvión de bailes nacidos entre adolescentes negros y popularizados por músicos negros (el Pony, el Watusi, el Mashed Potato, el Frug, el Monkey, el Jerk), cuyo nombre iba en el título del disco. Supusieron la vuelta del cuerpo a la cultura popular blanca. Los institucionalizaron las discotecas (el Whisky a Go Go del Sunset Strip, enero de 1964, con chicas bailando en jaulas) y los programas de televisión (Shindig!, Hullabaloo, Where the Action Is). «Land of 1000 Dances», de Chris Kenner (1962), enumeraba los bailes; Cannibal & the Headhunters, del este de Los Ángeles, le añadieron el «na na-ne-na-na» en 1965. En 1966 llegó el Boo-Ga-Loo de Tom and Jerrio, mezcla de Motown, aire latino y gritos a lo James Brown, en la estela de «Let’s Dance» de Chris Montez y «Wooly Bully» de Sam the Sham, el single más vendido de 1965.

refs.q: In the modern era, it all began with the Twist
refs.para: In the modern era, it all began with the Twist – the pop sensation of 1960, 1961 and 1962 and the great liberator of social dancing. It had taken about three years for the style to pass from a small group of young black Americans to a worldwide phenomenon, and, in the early to mid-sixties, other dances rushed in to fill the frantic need for more novelty – new beats, new steps, new names – that the Twist had created through its unexpected success.
refs.chapter: Julio: Land of 1000 Dances: Tamla, el soul y la Marcha contra el Miedo

refs.q: The Twist represented nothing less than the return of the body within mainstream American popular culture.
refs.para: ‘Keep loose’, ‘really feeling it’: these were powerful instructions to the white Americans targeted by the booklet. Most of the new dances originated among teenage blacks and were popularised by black musicians. Indeed, dance records would provide their entry into the pop charts. In turn, young whites were exposed to black culture as they rarely had been before. The Twist represented nothing less than the return of the body within mainstream American popular culture.
refs.chapter: Julio: Land of 1000 Dances: Tamla, el soul y la Marcha contra el Miedo

refs.q: There was another new dance craze in 1966: the Boo-Ga-Loo.
refs.para: There was another new dance craze in 1966: the Boo-Ga-Loo. This was popularised by a comedy/singing act called Tom and Jerrio, who saw kids performing the dance at a Chicago record hop. Released in March 1965, their single ‘Boo-Ga-Loo’ welded a fast Motown rhythm to a Latin feel and James Brown-style interjections. The record went to #11 in Billboard’s R&B charts, prompting a quick follow-up, ‘(Papa Chew) Do the Boo-Ga-Loo Part 1’.
refs.chapter: Julio: Land of 1000 Dances: Tamla, el soul y la Marcha contra el Miedo

podcast.body: The Twist dance craze was at its peak when The Ronettes, then underage, gained an accidental regular gig at the Peppermint Lounge in New York, a pivotal venue for the Twist. "They went to the peppermint lounge, just as the twist craze was at its height..."
